title: Prenatal exposure to arsenic and cadmium impacts infectious disease-related genes within the glucocorticoid receptor signal transduction pathway.
ehr_evidence: The study did not use EHR data; it re-analyzed published epigenomic, genomic, and proteomic datasets (DNA methylation, mRNA expression, protein expression) from twelve human pregnancy cohorts and queried databases including KEGG, the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD), Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA), and Genomatix.
summary: A bioinformatics meta-analysis using the Comparative Genomic Enrichment Method (CGEM) to identify 82 infection- and exposure-related genes enriched for the glucocorticoid receptor signal transduction pathway in the context of prenatal arsenic and cadmium exposure.
key_findings: A set of 82 infection and exposure-related (IER) genes was identified as overlapping between the infectious disease gene (IDG) database (n=1085) and the exposure responsive gene (ERG) database (n=950).
19 of the 82 IER genes were enriched for the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) signal transduction pathway (p = 1.58 × 10−18).
The TNFR1 pathway was enriched with 9 of 82 IER genes (p = 5.01 × 10−13).
The toll-like receptor (TLR) pathway was enriched with 8 of 82 IER genes (p = 6.31 × 10−13).
16 of the 82 (20%) IER genes play a role in all three major infectious disease pathways (viral, bacterial, parasitic).

Upstream regulator analysis identified enrichment for LPS (p = 4.98 × 10−38), CSF2 (p = 2.23 × 10−30), TNF (p = 9.72 × 10−30), poly(I:C) (p = 1.18 × 10−28), IL1β (p = 4.74 × 10−27), and NF-κB (p = 1.56 × 10−24).
CTD validation showed 50 of 82 (61%) IER genes are modulated by arsenic/iAs metabolites and 34 of 82 (41%) are modulated by cadmium.
Promoter analysis identified enrichment for negative glucocorticoid response elements (NGRE) (3.91 × 10−6) and NF-κB binding sites (3.72 × 10−14).
study_design: Bioinformatics meta-analysis / cross-study data re-analysis using the Comparative Genomic Enrichment Method (CGEM)
population: Human pregnancy cohorts (pregnant women and their fetuses/newborns) from Bangladesh, Mexico, the United States, and Thailand, with prenatal arsenic and cadmium exposure
limitations: Endpoints (DNA methylation, mRNA, protein expression) can be transient in response to toxic agents.
Some contributing studies had small sample sizes.
Incomplete analysis of possible confounders such as other environmental exposures.
Variations between studies in exposure duration and demographic information (age, gender, race).
Use of various biological media (blood, urine, nail clippings) to measure exposure.
The ERG list was derived solely from human pregnancy cohorts while CTD validation included in vitro and in vivo animal data.
